newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Weary space crew of damaged Mir granted a rest.
newsitem.headline: Weary space crew of damaged Mir granted a rest.

text.p: The crew of Russia's damaged Mir space station, who regained control after a self-inflicted crisis, were given a day of rest on Saturday while officials on Earth mulled the next step.

Mission director Vladimir Solovyov said Russians Vasily Tsibliyev and Alexander Lazutkin and American Michael Foale had been allowed free time to watch videos, read or listen to music and talk to their wives.

U.S. NASA astronaut Leroy Chiao told Reuters at Mission Control that the three were most likely to spend some time just looking at their home planet. "The most relaxing thing to do is to look out the window," he said. "It is a unique experience."

After struggling for 24 hours the crew arrested their crazy tumble through space caused by the failure of a computer unplugged by mistake on Thursday and locked the ship's solar panels onto the Sun, bringing lights and systems back to life.

But the latest incident seemed to convince ground controllers effectively to stand down the three cosmonauts, one of whom now has heart trouble, and wait for a relief crew to repair damage caused in a near-fatal collision last month.

Deputy mission director Sergei Krikalyov told reporters it was "very likely" the risky and complex repairs, already put off until next week because of commander Vasily Tsibliyev's stress-induced palpitations, would now have to wait until after the relief crew reached Mir on August 7.
Tsibliyev and Lazutkin had planned to return to Earth on August 26. British-born NASA physicist Foale is to go home aboard a U.S. Shuttle in September.

A meeting of officials at Mission Control outside Moscow on Monday may decide, however, that their mission is all but over, leaving them serving out the rest of their time on the stricken station as little more than caretakers.
Mir has been limping around on half power for the past three weeks, forcing the present crew to abandon their experiments and live a highly restricted, twilight existence.
Lazutkin on Friday played a crucial role in reconnecting most of Mir's life-support systems after one cosmonaut -- officials will not say who -- pulled out a cable and crashed the computer.
The computer crash disabled a gyro system that keeps Mir's solar panels lined up on the Sun, reducing the power supply to a minimum and forcing the crew to shut down all but vital systems.
The panels were being held in alignment by electronically controlled motors as Mir's batteries recharged.
Officials have said the gyroscope system, which uses no fuel at all, will be reconnected soon. The remaining systems can then be hooked up again.
